tagline: The old highway joins two shire towns between mountain ranges
intro: Historic Route 7A links Bennington and Manchester in the country between the Taconic and Green Mountains. Vermont Tourism includes the Shires of Vermont Byway among the state’s scenic routes, highlighting its mountain setting and the Batten Kill flowing through the valley. The road bends northeast between Arlington and Manchester and passes near Hildene, reached by Hildene Road. At Arlington, the Batten Kill turns west toward New York. The village occupies its south bank, with the Taconic Mountains to the west and Green Mountains to the east.

Before the limited-access US 7 opened, this was the route of US 7 itself. The Historic VT 7A signs distinguish that earlier alignment from the newer highway. The byway’s name describes a different arrangement: Bennington County has two shire towns, or county seats, with Manchester the North Shire and Bennington the South Shire. The old route still passes through Arlington village, while US 7 bypasses it to the east.

From Manchester Center, follow the old alignment south toward Arlington and Bennington. Hildene comes before Arlington, then South Shaftsbury and the Robert Frost Stone House. Old Bennington occupies a hill west of downtown; farther south, US 7 leads through Pownal toward Massachusetts.

moments.title: Hildene
moments.text: Hildene’s formal garden takes its pattern from a cathedral’s stained-glass window. Privet hedges draw the outlines, with flowering annuals and perennials supplying the colors. Planted in 1907, the garden followed the completion of Robert Todd Lincoln and Mary Harlan Lincoln’s summer house in 1905. The Georgian Revival house occupies a 300-foot promontory above the Battenkill Valley. Lincoln descendants lived here until 1975. Three years later, the Friends of Hildene bought the property and began restoring the house, outbuildings and gardens. Inside, the house is furnished almost entirely with Lincoln family furniture.
moments.notice: Privet hedges outline the garden’s stained-glass-window pattern.

moments.title: Robert Frost Stone House
moments.text: The young orchard at Robert Frost’s Stone House grew from trees grafted from one of his orchard’s last surviving apple trees. Frost bought the farm in 1920 with the goal of growing apples; during his residency, it included 80 acres and a large orchard. He also wrote “Stopping by Woods on a Snowy Evening” while living here. The house dates to 1769 and uses local stone and timber. The site now contains seven acres, stone walls and two barns, along with surviving apple trees. The Friends of Robert Frost restored the property after acquiring it in 2002.

moments.title: Old Bennington
moments.text: The Bennington Battle Monument marks the supplies the British sought, rather than the ground where the battle was fought. The fighting took place in Walloomsac, New York, in August 1777. The 306-foot stone obelisk was completed in 1889 after a local historical society began planning a centennial memorial. It shares Old Bennington’s hilltop historic district with the Old First Church, built in 1806 and restored in 1937. The district also preserves homes from the Revolutionary War era. The monument is built from blue-gray, fossil-bearing stone quarried in what is now Hudson Falls, New York.
